text:
₹22,000 crore of admitted liability and a settlement of around ₹6.5 crore is not a small matter. Those who are defending it are not the common citizens. 

After public anger, it was clarified from the Tribunal side that the final formal order had not yet been passed. But leave the legal jargon aside for a moment. The real story becomes much easier to understand when you simply follow the money, the guarantee and finally the voting.

Start from the beginning.

Subhash Chandra gave personal guarantees for loans taken by companies of his own group. At that time, wealth certificates showing more than ₹40,000 crore were submitted to lenders. So ask yourself a simple question. Was he giving personal guarantees for Tata or Ambani companies? No. These were his own group companies. The loan may not have entered his personal bank account, but it went into companies belonging to his own business ecosystem.

Suppose you own a company. You have personal wealth of ₹1 crore. You show the bank the strength of your company, show your own wealth, personally guarantee the loan and obtain ₹1 crore for your business. The money goes into your company account. Now if the company collapses, can you seriously say that you never took the money because it was not deposited into your savings account?

Now come to the second part of the story.

The companies start failing and the banks ask the Personal Guarantor to honour the guarantee. The man whose wealth had earlier been shown in tens of thousands of crores now says that very little personal wealth remains.

Naturally, the banks ask where did that wealth go? 

Then comes the most troubling part.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited, which had only about 1.98 percent voting share equivalent to 428 crore claim, suddenly approached the NCLT. Surprisingly, it later also voted in favour of this extremely small repayment plan and gets only Rs. 12.35 lakh. Shouldn't this party be investigated what deal it broke with debtors behind the curtain? 

And other creditors appear with claims even larger than those of banks. These creditors participate in voting on the repayment plan. The institutional lenders/Banks object and say that these entities are connected directly or indirectly with the Personal Guarantor and his family or business network, so their votes should not be allowed under Section 109.

Also, the Banks ask where did the Personal Guarantor wealth go. Before approving such an extraordinary settlement, should it not first be properly traced?

Now forget the law for one minute and just use common sense.

If an independent company is genuinely owed more than ₹1,000 crore, why would it happily accept ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore? For such a creditor, that amount is practically meaningless. Its natural interest would be to recover as much as possible not a meaningless amount.

So when creditors with enormous claims are willing to accept almost nothing, while independent banks oppose the plan, the obvious question is who these creditors really are and why their economic interest is so different from that of the banks.

Now take the same ₹1 crore example.

You owe the bank ₹1 crore. You say you now have only ₹30,000. You want a meagre settlement, you shrewdly influence a small investor with a deal and asks it to go NCLT. Then people connected with you arrive and say that you owe them ₹1.5 crore. They go to the Tribunal and say they are willing to settle their ₹1.5 crore claim for just ₹3000 and the NCLT approves it.

The bank says this makes no sense. These creditors are connected with the same guarantor.

But because those connected creditors have the larger voting share, their votes can decide the settlement.

Why shouldn't the same facility is available for every common citizen to reach a tribunal to settle their loan through voting and himself with his relatives, who declare they have bigger loans than banks, decide how much he wants to pay?

And that is exactly why Section 109 exists. Parliament did not want associates to vote on a repayment plan because otherwise a debtor or guarantor could influence his own settlement through connected creditors.

If the law is interpreted so narrowly and badly that connected entities can still dominate the vote simply because one formal ownership or control test is not satisfied, then the protection itself becomes meaningless.

That is the real issue here.

Not whether ₹22,000 crore went into Subhash Chandra’s personal account.

The real questions are much more serious.

Why was personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore shown when the guarantees were given?

Where did that wealth go?

Why were some creditors with huge claims willing to accept insignificant recoveries?

Why did institutional lenders oppose the plan?

And why should disputed connected creditors be allowed to hold decisive voting power over the settlement of the very person to whom they are connected?

Now ask yourself what this looks like.

Justice?

A clever use of legal technicalities?

Or a system that deserves a much deeper investigation before thousands of crores of institutional money are effectively written down?

The main fact every citizen should understand is this. 

No bank voted in favour of this plan.

Why? Because the banks are independent creditors and they are the ones actually losing money. And this is not the money of some faceless institution. It is the money of depositors, investors and ordinary citizens.

This is how the system works in India. The powerful take the benefit, the system bends for them, and the loss is quietly transferred to the public. In the end, common citizens pay for corruption, manipulation and loot, while the powerful become even richer.

@FinMinIndia @RBI @IBBIIndia @narendramodi @RahulGandhi @khurpenchh @NaukarshahiGems
#SubhashChandra #NCLT #NCLAT #IBC #Banking #ForensicAudit #CorporateGovernance #FinancialSystem #Accountability #BankingFraud

This Subhash Chandra insolvency case does not look like a normal commercial haircut to me. The deeper you read the NCLT record, the more uncomfortable the questions become.

Let’s understand the Maths.

The easiest defence being circulated in the Subhash Chandra insolvency case is that he was “only a guarantor.” That description is legally misleading.

Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of a surety is ordinarily coextensive with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise. In simple words, a personal guarantee is not a ceremonial signature. If the borrower defaults, the creditor can proceed against the guarantor for the guaranteed liability. That is precisely why claims of around ₹22,006 crore were admitted against Subhash Chandra in his personal insolvency proceeding.

And there is another important point. He was not a man worth ₹31 crore when these guarantees were being given. The NCLT record itself refers to net worth certificates showing approximately ₹45,888 crore in 2017 and ₹40,562 crore in 2018. So the story is not that a person worth ₹31 crore somehow guaranteed ₹22,000 crore. The real story is that a promoter who had represented personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore gave massive guarantees, and years later, when those guarantees became enforceable, his disclosed net worth had fallen to around ₹31.79 crore.

That immediately creates the first serious question.

Where did the wealth go?

If assets worth tens of thousands of crores disappeared from the personal balance sheet, then before granting an almost complete discharge of personal liability, the natural thing should have been to trace those assets properly. Which assets were sold, to whom, for what price, where did the consideration go, whether any assets moved to relatives, group entities, LLPs, trusts or connected companies, whether those transactions were at market value and what ultimately happened to the money.

This was not merely an outside suspicion. The Technical Member herself considered the fall in net worth serious enough to call for an independent forensic audit and asset tracing exercise.

Then comes the part which, to me, makes the case even more extraordinary.

Five disputed creditors, World Crest, Lemonade, Corpcall, Veena Investments and Direct Media, together controlled around 61.78 percent of the total voting power. Their links with the Chandra and Essel ecosystem through family relationships, directorships, shareholding and corporate connections were argued before the NCLT. The Technical Member found these connections serious enough to question their voting rights. The Third Member took a narrower statutory view and said the legal test to disqualify them as associates had not been fully satisfied.

But the mathematics does not disappear.

Around 77.48 percent of the total voting share supported the plan. Remove these five disputed creditors and the support falls to around 15.70 percent, while around 18.42 percent had voted against it.

So these five were not minor creditors sitting on the side.

Their votes were decisive.

Now understand why this matters economically.

Suppose a promoter has ₹10,000 crore of personal liability. A company within the same economic ecosystem holds a ₹6,000 crore claim and an outside bank holds a ₹4,000 crore claim. The connected company accepts almost nothing on its ₹6,000 crore claim and uses its voting strength to approve the plan.

On paper it looks like that company suffered a massive loss.

But if both sides are really part of the same economic pocket, then the internal claim is only being sacrificed on paper, while the same vote helps reduce or extinguish the outside bank’s ability to recover ₹4,000 crore personally from the promoter.

That is why the real question is not who took the biggest haircut on paper.

The real question is whose money was actually lost.

If these five creditors were genuinely independent and commercially separate, then their decision is one thing. But if their economic interests were aligned with Chandra or the Essel ecosystem, then their huge nominal claims could have supplied exactly the voting power needed to cut down the personal recovery rights of outside banks.

That possibility is exactly why beneficial ownership and real economic control should have been forensically examined before approving such a massive discharge.

And there is one more fact which makes it impossible to casually say that the entire process was flawless. Claims of more than ₹185 crore on behalf of 1,260 people were admitted without proper supporting documents and later had to be excluded by the Third Member.

So no, the real issue is not simply that ₹22,006 crore became ₹6.25 crore.

The deeper issue is this.

A person once represented as worth more than ₹40,000 crore came into personal insolvency with a disclosed net worth of around ₹31.79 crore. Five disputed creditors with documented links to the wider Chandra and Essel ecosystem held 61.78 percent of the voting power. Their votes were mathematically decisive. No complete independent forensic asset tracing was done before the plan was approved.

That is why “he was only a guarantor” is not an answer.

The two questions that must be answered are very simple.

Where did the wealth go?

And who really controlled the 61.78 percent voting block?

Until these two questions are answered through a proper forensic investigation, this will not look like an ordinary commercial haircut. It will remain a serious test of whether our insolvency system can actually deal with powerful promoters, connected entities and enormous financial claims without allowing form to defeat substance.

The original Dhruv Rathee video “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? | Kerala Story 2 EXPOSED” has already been withheld in India pursuant to the GAC Order dated 15.07.2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) passed after the Hon’ble Delhi High Court’s directions dated 03.07.2026 in W.P.(C) 8617/2026.

On 11.08.2026, the Hon’ble Delhi High Court granted us liberty to approach YouTube (R-3) if any re-upload of the same content appeared.

We wrote to YouTube on 14.08.2026 and shared the link of a video carrying the same offending content. Till date, YouTube has not taken it down.

See the audacity of Dhruv Rathee, when his original video was withheld, the same content was put up through another account, and YouTube has allowed it to remain.

This is continued, wilful non-compliance with a binding statutory order issued after the intervention of a Constitutional Court.

No intermediary is above the law. We are now constrained to seek further directions from the Hon’ble Delhi High Court.

The matter is listed today. 
@YouTube
@TeamYouTube

PUBLIC LEGAL NOTICE

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

2. THE GRIEVANCE OFFICER & LEGAL CELL
  Meta Platforms, Inc. / Instagram LLC
  (Intermediary hosting subject digital broadcast)

3. TO WHOMSOEVER IT MAY CONCERN / GENERAL PUBLIC
SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his guidance and support, and to the legal team for their efforts.

@OpIndia @TheBharatPost @TimesNow @SanatanPrabhat @MeghUpdates

I. அறிக்கையின் நோக்கம்

மேற்கு மாம்பலம், சென்னை பகுதியில் அமைந்துள்ள அருள்மிகு பாஷ்யகார ஆதிசென்ன கேசவ பெருமாள் திருக்கோயிலுக்குச் சொந்தமான நிலத்தில் ஏற்பட்டுள்ளதாகக் கூறப்படும் ஆக்கிரமிப்புகள், அவற்றை அகற்றுவது தொடர்பாக இந்து சமய அறநிலையத்துறை மேற்கொண்ட நடவடிக்கைகள், பின்னர் ஏற்பட்ட நிர்வாக நிலைப்பாட்டு மாற்றம் மற்றும் 03.09.2026 அன்று சென்னை உயர்நீதிமன்ற Division Bench வழங்கிய உத்தரவு ஆகியவற்றை சட்ட ரீதியாக ஆய்வு செய்வதே இவ்வறிக்கையின் நோக்கமாகும்.

இந்த அறிக்கையில் 2023, 2024 மற்றும் 2025 ஆண்டுகளில் இதே கோயில்/கோயில் நிலம் தொடர்பாக சென்னை உயர்நீதிமன்றத்தில் வெளிப்பட்ட முக்கிய வழக்குகளின் சட்டக் கொள்கைகளும், 03.09.2026 உத்தரவின் தாக்கமும் ஒருங்கிணைக்கப்படுகின்றன.

---

II. சம்பந்தப்பட்ட திருக்கோயில்

அருள்மிகு பாஷ்யகார ஆதிசென்ன கேசவ பெருமாள் திருக்கோயில், மேற்கு மாம்பலம், சென்னை என்பது பழமையான திருக்கோயிலாகும்.

2026-ஆம் ஆண்டு விசாரணையில், கோயில் 1,000 ஆண்டுகளுக்கும் மேற்பட்ட பழமையான heritage structure என நீதிமன்றத்தின் கவனத்திற்கு கொண்டு வரப்பட்டது.

எனவே, இக்கோயிலின் நிலச் சொத்துக்களைப் பாதுகாப்பது மட்டுமல்லாமல், கோயிலின் பாரம்பரிய கட்டமைப்பு மற்றும் தொல்லியல் முக்கியத்துவத்தையும் பாதுகாப்பது அவசியமாகிறது.

---

III. 2026-ஆம் ஆண்டு வழக்கின் பின்னணி

மேற்கு மாம்பலம் பகுதியில் கோயிலுக்குச் சொந்தமான நிலத்தில் நீண்டகாலமாக சில நபர்கள் வசித்து/பயன்படுத்தி வருவதாகக் கூறப்பட்டது.

இந்த ஆக்கிரமிப்புகள் தொடர்பாக கோயில் நிர்வாகமும் HR&CE துறையும் முன்னதாக நடவடிக்கை மேற்கொண்டிருந்தன.

முக்கியமாக, குறித்த நிலம்:

1. பக்தர்களுக்கான அன்னதானக் கூடம் அமைக்கவும்;
2. பக்தர்களின் வாகன வசதிக்காக இருசக்கர வாகன நிறுத்துமிடம் ஏற்படுத்தவும்

தேவைப்படுவதாக முன்பு நிர்வாகத்தின் சார்பில் தெரிவிக்கப்பட்டிருந்தது.

---

IV. 18 ஆக்கிரமிப்பாளர்கள்

03.09.2026 விசாரணையின்போது, குறித்த கோயில் நிலத்தில் மொத்தம் 18 ஆக்கிரமிப்பாளர்கள் இருப்பது தொடர்பாக நீதிமன்றத்தின் கவனத்திற்கு கொண்டு வரப்பட்டது.

முன்னதாக சிலர் வெளியேற்றப்பட்டிருந்தாலும், மீதமுள்ள ஆக்கிரமிப்பாளர்களை வெளியேற்றும் நடவடிக்கை முழுமையாக நிறைவு பெறவில்லை.

இதனால், கோயில் நிலத்தை முழுமையாக மீட்பது தொடர்பாக நீதிமன்றம் நேரடியாக தலையிட வேண்டிய சூழ்நிலை ஏற்பட்டது.

---

V. C. Janarthanan அவர்களின் மனு

இந்த விவகாரம் C. Janarthanan அவர்களால் சென்னை உயர்நீதிமன்றத்தின் கவனத்திற்கு கொண்டு வரப்பட்டது.

மனுவின் அடிப்படை நோக்கம்:

«கோயிலுக்குச் சொந்தமான நிலத்தில் உள்ள ஆக்கிரமிப்புகளை அகற்றி, அந்நிலத்தை கோயில் மற்றும் பக்தர்களின் நலனுக்காகப் பயன்படுத்துவதற்கு உரிய நடவடிக்கை எடுக்க வேண்டும்.»

என்பதாகும்.

இந்த வழக்கு நீதிபதிகள் G. Jayachandran மற்றும் E. Manoharan அடங்கிய Division Bench முன்பு விசாரணைக்கு வந்தது.

---

VI. HR&CE துறையின் முந்தைய நிலைப்பாடு

ஆக்கிரமிப்புகளை அகற்றுவதற்கு முன்பு HR&CE நிர்வாகம் எடுத்திருந்த நிலைப்பாடு தெளிவானதாக இருந்தது.

கோயில் நிலம் மீட்கப்பட்ட பின்னர்:

- Annadhanam facility;
- Devotee parking facility;

போன்ற பயன்பாடுகளுக்கு அந்நிலத்தை பயன்படுத்த திட்டமிடப்பட்டதாக நீதிமன்றத்தில் தெரிவிக்கப்பட்டிருந்தது.

இதனால், கோயில் நிலத்தை தனிநபர் பயன்பாட்டிலிருந்து மீட்டு, கோயிலின் சமய மற்றும் பக்தர் நலப் பயன்பாட்டிற்கு கொண்டுவருவதே நிர்வாகத்தின் ஆரம்ப நோக்கமாக இருந்தது.

---

VII. நிர்வாக நிலைப்பாட்டில் ஏற்பட்ட மாற்றம்

03.09.2026 விசாரணையில் Executive Officer சார்பில் புதிய status report தாக்கல் செய்யப்பட்டது.

அதில், சில occupants நிலுவையில் இருந்த தொகையின் ஒரு பகுதியை செலுத்தியுள்ளதாகவும், அவர்களை தொடர்ந்து அங்கு இருக்க அனுமதிப்பது தொடர்பாக நிர்வாகத்தில் மாற்று நிலைப்பாடு உருவாகியுள்ளதாகவும் தெரிவிக்கப்பட்டது.

மேலும், முன்பு ஆக்கிரமிப்புகளை அகற்றி அந்த நிலத்தில் அன்னதானக் கூடம் அமைக்க வேண்டும் என்ற திட்டத்திற்குப் பதிலாக, அன்னதானக் கூடத்தை கோயில் வளாகத்துக்குள் அமைப்பது போன்ற மாற்று யோசனையும் முன்வைக்கப்பட்டது.

Department attempts to penalise an Independent Director under GST Section 122(1A); Bombay High Court steps in to grant interim protection against coercive recovery.

Issue:
Whether an individual serving as an Independent Director of a company comes within the scope of penalty provisions under Section 122(1A) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, and whether interim protection against coercive recovery is warranted.

Rule:
Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act, 2017 prescribes penal liability only on any person who retains the benefit of specified fraudulent transactions or at whose instance such transactions are conducted; as judicially interpreted by the Coordinate Bench in Shantanu Sanjay Hundekari, an individual acting in a non-beneficiary or official capacity does not automatically fall under the sweep of this section.

Application:
The Assessee was subjected to penalty proceedings under Section 122(1A) in an individual capacity while serving merely as an Independent Director of the company. The Assessee contended that he was not the company itself nor did he fall within the ambit of the penal provision, relying upon the Coordinate Bench ruling which had attained finality as the Supreme Court did not interfere with it. Upon examining the statutory provision and binding precedent, the High Court observed that a strong prima facie case was established in favour of the Assessee.

Conclusion:
Since a strong prima facie case was made out by the Assessee based on established judicial precedent, the High Court granted ad-interim relief and directed the Department not to take any coercive action regarding the penalty in question until further orders.

Impact Analysis:
This order reaffirms that the Department cannot routinely invoke Section 122(1A) against independent directors or corporate professionals in their individual capacities, offering vital interim immunity from coercive tax recovery where no direct personal involvement or retention of illicit benefit is established.

₹22,000 crore of admitted liability and a settlement of around ₹6.5 crore is not a small matter. Those who are defending it are not the common citizens. 

After public anger, it was clarified from the Tribunal side that the final formal order had not yet been passed. But leave the legal jargon aside for a moment. The real story becomes much easier to understand when you simply follow the money, the guarantee and finally the voting.

Start from the beginning.

Subhash Chandra gave personal guarantees for loans taken by companies of his own group. At that time, wealth certificates showing more than ₹40,000 crore were submitted to lenders. So ask yourself a simple question. Was he giving personal guarantees for Tata or Ambani companies? No. These were his own group companies. The loan may not have entered his personal bank account, but it went into companies belonging to his own business ecosystem.

Suppose you own a company. You have personal wealth of ₹1 crore. You show the bank the strength of your company, show your own wealth, personally guarantee the loan and obtain ₹1 crore for your business. The money goes into your company account. Now if the company collapses, can you seriously say that you never took the money because it was not deposited into your savings account?

Now come to the second part of the story.

The companies start failing and the banks ask the Personal Guarantor to honour the guarantee. The man whose wealth had earlier been shown in tens of thousands of crores now says that very little personal wealth remains.

Naturally, the banks ask where did that wealth go? 

Then comes the most troubling part.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited, which had only about 1.98 percent voting share equivalent to 428 crore claim, suddenly approached the NCLT. Surprisingly, it later also voted in favour of this extremely small repayment plan and gets only Rs. 12.35 lakh. Shouldn't this party be investigated what deal it broke with debtors behind the curtain? 

And other creditors appear with claims even larger than those of banks. These creditors participate in voting on the repayment plan. The institutional lenders/Banks object and say that these entities are connected directly or indirectly with the Personal Guarantor and his family or business network, so their votes should not be allowed under Section 109.

Also, the Banks ask where did the Personal Guarantor wealth go. Before approving such an extraordinary settlement, should it not first be properly traced?

Now forget the law for one minute and just use common sense.

If an independent company is genuinely owed more than ₹1,000 crore, why would it happily accept ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore? For such a creditor, that amount is practically meaningless. Its natural interest would be to recover as much as possible not a meaningless amount.

So when creditors with enormous claims are willing to accept almost nothing, while independent banks oppose the plan, the obvious question is who these creditors really are and why their economic interest is so different from that of the banks.

Now take the same ₹1 crore example.

You owe the bank ₹1 crore. You say you now have only ₹30,000. You want a meagre settlement, you shrewdly influence a small investor with a deal and asks it to go NCLT. Then people connected with you arrive and say that you owe them ₹1.5 crore. They go to the Tribunal and say they are willing to settle their ₹1.5 crore claim for just ₹3000 and the NCLT approves it.

The bank says this makes no sense. These creditors are connected with the same guarantor.

But because those connected creditors have the larger voting share, their votes can decide the settlement.

Why shouldn't the same facility is available for every common citizen to reach a tribunal to settle their loan through voting and himself with his relatives, who declare they have bigger loans than banks, decide how much he wants to pay?

And that is exactly why Section 109 exists. Parliament did not want associates to vote on a repayment plan because otherwise a debtor or guarantor could influence his own settlement through connected creditors.

If the law is interpreted so narrowly and badly that connected entities can still dominate the vote simply because one formal ownership or control test is not satisfied, then the protection itself becomes meaningless.

That is the real issue here.

Not whether ₹22,000 crore went into Subhash Chandra’s personal account.

The real questions are much more serious.

Why was personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore shown when the guarantees were given?

Where did that wealth go?

Why were some creditors with huge claims willing to accept insignificant recoveries?

Why did institutional lenders oppose the plan?

And why should disputed connected creditors be allowed to hold decisive voting power over the settlement of the very person to whom they are connected?

Now ask yourself what this looks like.

Justice?

A clever use of legal technicalities?

Or a system that deserves a much deeper investigation before thousands of crores of institutional money are effectively written down?

The main fact every citizen should understand is this. 

No bank voted in favour of this plan.

Why? Because the banks are independent creditors and they are the ones actually losing money. And this is not the money of some faceless institution. It is the money of depositors, investors and ordinary citizens.

This is how the system works in India. The powerful take the benefit, the system bends for them, and the loss is quietly transferred to the public. In the end, common citizens pay for corruption, manipulation and loot, while the powerful become even richer.

This Subhash Chandra insolvency case does not look like a normal commercial haircut to me. The deeper you read the NCLT record, the more uncomfortable the questions become.

Let’s understand the Maths.

The easiest defence being circulated in the Subhash Chandra insolvency case is that he was “only a guarantor.” That description is legally misleading.

Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of a surety is ordinarily coextensive with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise. In simple words, a personal guarantee is not a ceremonial signature. If the borrower defaults, the creditor can proceed against the guarantor for the guaranteed liability. That is precisely why claims of around ₹22,006 crore were admitted against Subhash Chandra in his personal insolvency proceeding.

And there is another important point. He was not a man worth ₹31 crore when these guarantees were being given. The NCLT record itself refers to net worth certificates showing approximately ₹45,888 crore in 2017 and ₹40,562 crore in 2018. So the story is not that a person worth ₹31 crore somehow guaranteed ₹22,000 crore. The real story is that a promoter who had represented personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore gave massive guarantees, and years later, when those guarantees became enforceable, his disclosed net worth had fallen to around ₹31.79 crore.

That immediately creates the first serious question.

Where did the wealth go?

If assets worth tens of thousands of crores disappeared from the personal balance sheet, then before granting an almost complete discharge of personal liability, the natural thing should have been to trace those assets properly. Which assets were sold, to whom, for what price, where did the consideration go, whether any assets moved to relatives, group entities, LLPs, trusts or connected companies, whether those transactions were at market value and what ultimately happened to the money.

This was not merely an outside suspicion. The Technical Member herself considered the fall in net worth serious enough to call for an independent forensic audit and asset tracing exercise.

Then comes the part which, to me, makes the case even more extraordinary.

Five disputed creditors, World Crest, Lemonade, Corpcall, Veena Investments and Direct Media, together controlled around 61.78 percent of the total voting power. Their links with the Chandra and Essel ecosystem through family relationships, directorships, shareholding and corporate connections were argued before the NCLT. The Technical Member found these connections serious enough to question their voting rights. The Third Member took a narrower statutory view and said the legal test to disqualify them as associates had not been fully satisfied.

But the mathematics does not disappear.

Around 77.48 percent of the total voting share supported the plan. Remove these five disputed creditors and the support falls to around 15.70 percent, while around 18.42 percent had voted against it.

So these five were not minor creditors sitting on the side.

Their votes were decisive.

Now understand why this matters economically.

Suppose a promoter has ₹10,000 crore of personal liability. A company within the same economic ecosystem holds a ₹6,000 crore claim and an outside bank holds a ₹4,000 crore claim. The connected company accepts almost nothing on its ₹6,000 crore claim and uses its voting strength to approve the plan.

On paper it looks like that company suffered a massive loss.

But if both sides are really part of the same economic pocket, then the internal claim is only being sacrificed on paper, while the same vote helps reduce or extinguish the outside bank’s ability to recover ₹4,000 crore personally from the promoter.

That is why the real question is not who took the biggest haircut on paper.

The real question is whose money was actually lost.

If these five creditors were genuinely independent and commercially separate, then their decision is one thing. But if their economic interests were aligned with Chandra or the Essel ecosystem, then their huge nominal claims could have supplied exactly the voting power needed to cut down the personal recovery rights of outside banks.

That possibility is exactly why beneficial ownership and real economic control should have been forensically examined before approving such a massive discharge.

And there is one more fact which makes it impossible to casually say that the entire process was flawless. Claims of more than ₹185 crore on behalf of 1,260 people were admitted without proper supporting documents and later had to be excluded by the Third Member.

So no, the real issue is not simply that ₹22,006 crore became ₹6.25 crore.

The deeper issue is this.

A person once represented as worth more than ₹40,000 crore came into personal insolvency with a disclosed net worth of around ₹31.79 crore. Five disputed creditors with documented links to the wider Chandra and Essel ecosystem held 61.78 percent of the voting power. Their votes were mathematically decisive. No complete independent forensic asset tracing was done before the plan was approved.

That is why “he was only a guarantor” is not an answer.

The two questions that must be answered are very simple.

Where did the wealth go?

And who really controlled the 61.78 percent voting block?

Until these two questions are answered through a proper forensic investigation, this will not look like an ordinary commercial haircut. It will remain a serious test of whether our insolvency system can actually deal with powerful promoters, connected entities and enormous financial claims without allowing form to defeat substance.

Validity of Demand against a Dead Person..!! Section 93

Research & Thoughts: Abhishek Raja Ram; 9810638155

1. Venus Trading Co. vs State of U.P. - Allahabad High Court
2025-VIL-919-ALH

GST Law Does Not Permit Tax Determination against a Dead Person And Recovery Thereof from Legal Heirs. The order is invalid since it was made without notifying the legal representative.

2. Amit Kumar Sethia (DECEASED) vs State of Uttar Pradesh - Allahabad High Court
(2025) 29 CENTAX 182

Where show cause notice was issued and determination was made and impugned order was passed under Section 73(9) of GST Act in name of a dead person without issuing notice to legal representative, impugned order was to be set aside. ARR

3. Sayan Biswas vs Union of India - Calcutta High Court
(2024) 21 CENTAX 167

Where show cause notice was issued on registered taxpayer and such taxpayer passed away prior to date of personal hearing, subsequent order confirming demand was nullity; proper officer was to be directed to dispose of proceedings after affording opportunity of hearing to legal heir. ARR

4. Arvind Traders vs State of Uttar Pradesh - Allahabad High Court
(2025) 4 TaxReply 13022

The court held that issuing a SCN and determining a tax demand directly against a deceased person is impermissible. (ARR) While Section 93 of the GST Act provides that legal representatives can be liable for tax dues if the business is continued or discontinued after the death of the proprietor, it does not authorise initiating proceedings or making determinations against the deceased individual.

5. Sushil Kumar Kesarwani vs State of Uttar Pradesh - Allahabad High Court
(2025) TAXONATION 828

The court invalidated a GST demand against a deceased proprietor, emphasising that recovery can't proceed without notifying the legal representative. Section 93 allows recovery from heirs, but not the determination of liability against the deceased. Legal representatives must be notified and allowed to respond before action. The demand, made without notifying the heir, was thus set aside. ARR

6. Sahaya Kapil Bosco vs Deputy State Tax Officer, Nagercoil - Madras High Court
(2025) 175 taxmann com 727

Assessment order passed against deceased person without hearing legal heir, was to be set aside and fresh order was to be passed after reply to show cause notice was filed by legal heir.

M/s. Columbia Sportswear India Sourcing Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India [WP: 2025:KHC:17354] - Karnataka High Court

The Courts held that providing direct business advisory, technical, or sourcing assistance to foreign clients on a principal-to-principal basis does not render a firm an "intermediary" under Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act. Impact: Establishes that direct services supplied to overseas entities qualify as zero-rated "export of services" under IGST. Indian service providers can claim full refunds of unutilized ITC rather than being subjected to local GST.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

USCIRF Commissioner Asif Mahmood wants "dialogue" with RSS when he has lost the debate on FACTS. 

THIS IS AN EXHAUSTIVE LINE-BY-LINE 7-PT TAKEDOWN OF HIS USCIRF REPORT ON RSS, MODI & INDIA.

1. RSS “SUBGROUPS” & VIOLENCE

MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF CONFLATION:
“Members of RSS subgroups have perpetrated violent attacks against religious minorities, including Christians, Dalits, Muslims, and Sikhs.”

WHY IT'S A DOUBLE STANDARD:
USCIRF says “members of RSS subgroups”, not that the RSS ordered, funded or organised these attacks. If the conduct of a member or affiliate automatically establishes the culpability of the parent organisation, then should the Cong party be held institutionally responsible for 1984 anti-Sikh riots where Cong leaders were convicted?

2. “HINDUTVA INHERENTLY DISCRIMINATES”
MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“The BJP has enforced policies that closely align with the RSS' Hindutva ideology, inherently discriminating against religious minority communities.”

WHY IT'S A SWEEPING STATEMENT WITHOUT EVIDENCE:
“Inherently discriminating” is a conclusion. Where has USCIRF identified specific discriminatory provisions. Infact, under BJP rule in Karnataka, when backward-class categories were reorganised in 2023, Christians and Jains remained eligible for reservation under Category 2D

3. “RSS SEEKS TO EXCLUDE NON-HINDUS”

UNSUBSTANTIATED USCIRF ACCUSATION:
The RSS promotes a Hindu 'Rastra' that excludes Muslims, Christians, Jews, Buddhists, Parsis and other religious communities.

WHY IT'S TOO BROAD:
Where is the RSS resolution saying “Muslims cannot be citizens,” “Christians cannot hold office,” or “non-Hindus must lose constitutional rights”? In fact RSS engages minorities through Muslim Rashtriya Manch.

4. CAA = ANTI-MUSLIM CITIZENSHIP LAW

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
The government has discriminated against Muslims through the Citizenship Amendment Act.

WHY ITS FACTUALLY WRONG:
The CAA creates an accelerated citizenship route for specified persecuted minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. It does not contain a provision stripping an INDIAN Muslim of existing CITIZENSHIP. In any case the CAA draws upon the logic of U.S. laws like the Lautenberg-Specter Amendment.

5. NRC “FORCIBLY EXPELLED MUSLIM CITIZENS”

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“Authorities have also forcefully expelled Muslim citizens in Assam under the National Register of Citizens (NRC) and Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA).”

WHY IT'S FACTUALLY WRONG:
The Assam NRC was published in 2019, but the legal process has not been operationalised to the point USCIRF's language suggests. The Gauhati High Court has recorded that the final NRC has not been notified in the Official Gazette, has not been given effect by the Government of India, and rejection slips have not been issued.

6. FCRA = THREAT TO FAITH-BASED ORGANISATIONS

USCIRF ACCUSATION:
“Pending amendments to the FCRA [are] threatening the ability of faith-based organizations to continue their operations in the country.”

WHY IT'S MISLEADING:
FCRA regulates foreign contributions, not religious belief or the right to practise religion. Faith-based organisations can operate in India; the question is whether and under what conditions they can receive foreign funding. The United States itself has FARA, which regulates certain activities undertaken on behalf of foreign principals. If the U.S. can, why can't India?

7. UMAR KHALID = PERSECUTED FOR BEING MUSLIM

MISCHIEVOUS USCIRF CONFLATION:
“Religious minorities—like Umar Khalid, who has been detained since 2020 for leading peaceful protests opposing the religiously discriminatory CAA—often spend years in jail without a trial.”
WHY IT'S SLANDER:
USCIRF presents Khalid's detention as though he were imprisoned for opposing the CAA.
But SC'S Jan 2026 order records the prosecution material alleging that Khalid played a “central and formative role” in the violence and mobilisation.

What if I told you ripple:native just moved closer to a financial universe doing $17.5 TRILLION in FX and interest-rate derivatives every single day?

I’m not talking about some random prediction.

I’m talking about BIS Working Paper No. 1374.

This is going to be a long read, because the headline barely scratches the surface.

Four of the five authors work at the Bank for International Settlements, and instead of only mentioning XRP Ledger in theory, the researchers actually built, tested and published an open-source XRPL-based prototype.

That distinction matters.

This is a research implementation, not a production BIS deployment.

But the technical choice itself is what caught me.

The researchers needed a public blockchain that could help prove official economic and financial data had not been altered.

They chose XRP Ledger.

And they explained why:

low fees, fast finality, developer resources and existing research around its consensus system.

This wasn’t somebody adding an XRP logo to a presentation.

They built the gateway.

They created XRPL transactions.

They used institutional anchoring wallets.

They put cryptographic proofs inside transaction memos.

They linked publisher identities to XRPL addresses.

They retrieved those transactions again during verification.

Then they measured how the system performed.

Median publication latency came in around 3–5 seconds.

Verification took around 1–2 seconds.

That is where my brain immediately went beyond the headline.

Because what exactly were they trying to verify?

The kind of information the entire financial system runs on.

-Inflation.
-GDP.
-Interest rates.
-Banking statistics.
-Debt information.
-Financial-stability data.
-Regulatory reporting.

Imagine a central bank publishes an inflation number.

Today that number gets copied everywhere.

-Websites.
-News terminals.
-Databases.
-Screenshots.
-AI models.
-Trading systems.

Once it spreads across the internet, how does another machine independently prove that the number it received is exactly what the institution originally published?

That is the problem BIS researchers were attacking.

Their model creates a cryptographic fingerprint of the official dataset.

Individual statistical series can receive fingerprints too.

Those hashes are combined through a Merkle tree.

A final Merkle root gets anchored to XRPL.

The underlying economic data do not need to be dumped onto the blockchain.

XRPL simply keeps the proof.

Think of it like this:

The official institution publishes the document.

XRPL holds the tamper-proof receipt.

Someone changes even one part of the underlying file?

The cryptographic fingerprint changes.

Now a bank, regulator, investor, trading engine or AI agent can check:

Is this the original data?

Has it been changed?

Did it really come from the institution claiming to publish it?

And that second part is where this paper gets even more serious.

The BIS prototype combines the data proof with a W3C Verifiable Credential for the publisher.

The publisher’s cryptographic identity is connected to an XRPL address.

The paper even uses the format:

did:xrpl:<address>

So you are not only verifying the information.

You are verifying who published it.

Now picture a financial world where machines can check both automatically.

A central bank publishes CPI.

A model receives it.

Before touching money, the software checks XRPL.

Correct file.

Correct publisher.

No alteration.

Then it acts.

That sounds simple until you realize what financial markets actually do with official data.

-Rates move.
-Currencies move.
-Bond prices move.
-Derivatives reprice.
-Collateral requirements change.
-Loans reset.
-Inflation-linked instruments adjust.
-Portfolio risk changes.

And this is where BIS Working Paper 1374 stops being a boring statistics paper for me.

Because the authors themselves discuss putting verified information beside digital financial assets.

They specifically mention:

-CBDCs
-stablecoins
-tokenized deposits
-derivatives.

That one section changes the entire way I look at this.

The vision is not simply:

“Put a hash on a blockchain.”

It becomes:

verified economic information + digital money + tokenized assets + automated execution.

Now remember what Ripple has been building around XRPL.

-Multi-Purpose Tokens.
-Credentials.
-Permissioned Domains.
-Permissioned DEX infrastructure.
-Confidential Transfers.
-Stablecoins.
-Institutional lending.
-Tokenized collateral.
-FX.
-Onchain credit.

And Ripple has repeatedly positioned XRP across payments, liquidity and credit.

Now put those pieces beside what the BIS researchers are exploring.

An official institution needs an identity.

XRPL can represent identity and credentials.

A regulated participant needs permission to enter a market.

XRPL is building permissioned infrastructure.

A bond needs trustworthy economic information.

The BIS prototype shows one way that information can be authenticated through XRPL.

A financial asset needs a digital representation.

XRPL is being built for tokenization.

A transaction needs money.

Stablecoins and tokenized deposits can provide the cash side.

Then all those different assets need liquidity.

That is where ripple:native becomes much more interesting to me.

But before getting there, look at the scale surrounding BIS itself.

The BIS does not process the world’s $9.6 trillion of daily FX transactions.

It measures that market through its Triennial Central Bank Survey.

That distinction matters.

According to the numbers in the context here:

global OTC FX turnover = $9.6 TRILLION every day.

Then add:

OTC interest-rate derivatives turnover = $7.9 TRILLION every day.

Together:

$17.5 TRILLION per day.

Just the FX number annualized across roughly 250 trading days comes to around:

$2.4 QUADRILLION per year.

That is the financial universe BIS research sits over.

-Currencies.
-Banks.
-Central banks.
-FX swaps.
-Rates.
-Derivatives.
-Cross-border capital.
-Collateral.
-Dollar funding.

And researchers inside that institution just chose XRP Ledger for an actual technical prototype.

That is why I keep telling people not to reduce this to transaction fees.

Yes, the worked example uses an XRPL Payment transaction.

Yes, the reference cost is only:

10 drops = 0.00001 XRP.

Yes, transaction fees on XRPL are destroyed.

So if this kind of anchoring eventually ran on mainnet, publishing data itself would consume XRP.

But that is not the part that gets me excited.

The fee is intentionally tiny.

The much bigger question is:

What happens when verified information starts triggering financial activity on the same broader infrastructure?

The paper itself talks about:

inflation-linked products

perpetual futures

tokenized financial instruments

derivative settlement

interest payments

automated compliance

and even:

automated monetary-policy applications.

Now we are talking about information causing money to move.

Imagine an inflation-linked bond.

The government publishes inflation.

That release gets cryptographically anchored.

The bond checks the proof.

The CPI number is verified.

The contract adjusts what is owed.

Digital cash settles the payment.

No one has to manually copy a number from a website into another system.

No one has to blindly trust a third-party data feed.

The financial instrument can verify the economic input itself.

That is the idea I keep coming back to:

self-verifying finance.

And the researchers even discuss using the XRPL EVM-compatible sidechain for more advanced applications where data verification and programmable financial execution exist in the same broader ecosystem.

They mention:

access controls,

permissioning,

automated compliance,

multisignature requirements,

oracle integration,

programmable validation.

Now connect that with Ripple’s institutional roadmap.

Credentials can prove who a participant is.

Permissioned Domains can define who belongs inside a regulated environment.

Tokenized assets can represent financial instruments.

RLUSD can represent digital dollar liquidity.

Lending can make those assets productive.

XRP can provide native network resources and, where economically useful, liquidity between fragmented assets.

That is a very different picture of XRPL than the one people were arguing about years ago.

It is not simply:

“Can XRP send a payment quickly?”

The question becomes:

Can XRPL sit underneath parts of a machine-readable financial system?

And Working Paper 1374 just gave that question much more weight for me.

There is another section that barely gets discussed.

The architecture is not limited to one data publisher.

The researchers designed a multi-publisher system.

Different institutions can create their own Merkle roots.

Those roots can be combined into one larger super-root.

One XRPL transaction can anchor that shared proof.

Yet each publisher remains independently accountable for its own data.

Now imagine the participants.

Central Bank A.

Central Bank B.

Regulator C.

Statistical Office D.

International Organization E.

One public verification system.

Different publishers.

Independent cryptographic accountability.

That begins to resemble infrastructure for cross-border public-sector data exchange.

And the paper’s own conclusion talks about trustworthy exchange among:

national statistical offices

central banks

international organizations.

Then look at who already uses the statistical standard the paper builds around.

SDMX is sponsored by institutions including:

BIS

European Central Bank

Eurostat

International Monetary Fund

OECD

United Nations

World Bank Group

International Labour Organization.

That does not mean those institutions are adopting XRPL.

But it tells you something important about the design philosophy.

The researchers did not create a blockchain system that requires the existing financial world to throw everything away.

They designed it to sit underneath an existing institutional standard.

That matters a lot.

Because the easiest technology to adopt is often the technology that does not force everyone to rebuild from zero.

Existing systems can continue publishing.

XRPL can provide the cryptographic proof underneath.

Then comes BIS Open Tech.

The paper says the open-source reference implementation is being released as a prototype through BIS Open Tech and the SDMX community.

That means other institutions can inspect it.

Reuse it.

Modify it.

Build on it.

This is how technical ideas can spread inside serious institutions.

Not through hype.

Through code.

Documentation.

Standards.

Reuse.

That is the kind of adoption path I pay attention to.

Then there is the AI angle.

This is where the whole thesis becomes almost unfairly interesting.

The authors explicitly discuss AI agents.

An AI system receives economic information.

Instead of blindly trusting what it scraped from somewhere, it can ask:

Is this data authentic?

It checks the XRPL proof.

Valid?

Continue.

Invalid?

Do nothing.

Now compare that with what Ripple launched in June 2026:

the XRPL AI Starter Kit, designed around autonomous agents making payments with XRP and RLUSD.

Two completely separate directions suddenly sit beside each other.

BIS research:

AI verifies information through XRPL.

Ripple ecosystem:

AI moves value through XRPL.

Now imagine both ideas eventually meeting.

An agent receives official inflation data.

It verifies the release cryptographically.

It recalculates risk.

It reprices a bond.

It adjusts collateral.

It changes an FX position.

It executes a payment.

It settles in RLUSD.

It routes through XRP where XRP is the best available liquidity path.

That is machine-native finance.

And now go back to the scale.

The BIS 2025 Triennial Survey says:

$9.6T/day FX.

The dollar appears on one side of 89% of FX trades.

The euro is involved in 28.9%.

The Japanese yen in 16.8%.

FX swaps alone are around $4T every day.

Then another $7.9T/day exists in OTC interest-rate derivatives turnover.

Think about what happens if only part of those markets becomes tokenized.

Digital USD deposits.

Digital EUR deposits.

Tokenized JPY.

RLUSD.

CBDCs.

Tokenized Treasuries.

Interest-rate derivatives.

FX derivatives.

Collateral.

Money-market instruments.

The first problem is getting the assets onchain.

The second is verifying the information those assets depend on.

The third is moving liquidity between all the different forms of value.

This BIS paper attacks the second problem using XRPL.

Ripple has spent years attacking the first and third.

That is why the combination gets my attention.

And you do not need XRPL to capture the whole market for the numbers to become enormous.

For scale only:

0.1% of $9.6T daily FX turnover = $9.6B per day.

1% = $96B per day.

Again, that is not a forecast.

It shows what even tiny percentages mean when the underlying market is measured in trillions every day.

And that is only FX.

It does not include the additional $7.9T/day of interest-rate derivatives turnover BIS measures.

This is where the XRP liquidity thesis changes from a crypto argument into a market-structure argument.

Suppose the future has hundreds of tokenized currencies and financial products.

Every possible pair cannot maintain perfect direct liquidity.

USD token / EUR token.

EUR token / JPY token.

JPY token / RLUSD.

RLUSD / Treasury token.

Treasury token / derivative.

Derivative / deposit token.

The combinations explode.

A common intermediate asset becomes useful whenever routing through it provides a better market.

That is where XRP’s role becomes interesting.

Not replacing the dollar.

Not replacing the euro.

Not replacing CBDCs.

Not replacing bank deposits.

Connecting liquidity between them when that route makes economic sense.

Now imagine the system is automated.

No trader needs to shout:

“Use XRP.”

Software looks at:

price,

spread,

depth,

settlement,

availability.

If the XRP path wins, the software uses XRP.

That is the outcome I care about.

Machine-selected liquidity.

And if those transactions grow large enough, the XRP market itself has to change.

Institutional market makers need inventory.

Liquidity providers need inventory.

Prime brokers need financing capacity.

Order books need deeper capital.

Large transactions need to clear without huge price impact.

That is where the price thesis becomes different from retail speculation.

If XRP ever helps support institutional flows inside markets measured in trillions per day, the relevant question is not:

“How many retail holders bought today?”

It becomes:

How much dollar liquidity does the XRP market need to represent?

That is an entirely different valuation conversation.

There is one more thing I think people are missing.

BIS Working Paper 1374 does not only talk about SDMX statistics.

The researchers say the same architecture can extend to:

XBRL

regulatory filings

FINREP

COREP

and other forms of structured official information.

Now imagine banks submitting regulatory reports that receive immutable XRPL proofs.

The bank cannot quietly change an old filing later.

The regulator can verify the exact version.

Auditors can verify it.

Another authority can verify it.

AI software can consume it.

One system can prove both:

who submitted the data

and

whether it changed.

That gives XRPL a potential role far beyond payments.

It starts touching the information layer of finance.

And this is why the line “BIS used XRP Ledger” actually undersells the paper.

What happened is more specific.

Researchers inside BIS took a real institutional problem.

They selected XRPL.

They built a working implementation.

They measured performance.

They published the code direction.

Then they explored how authenticated data could coexist with:

CBDCs,

stablecoins,

tokenized deposits,

derivatives,

AI agents,

automated financial instruments.

That is what I am bullish on.

Not a logo.

Not a rumor.

Not a screenshot.

Technical work.

And when I look at the direction Ripple is independently pushing XRPL, the overlap is hard for me to ignore.

Trusted identities.

Verified information.

Regulated participants.

Tokenized assets.

Digital money.

Automated execution.

Credit.

Collateral.

FX.

Liquidity.

AI.

Put together, the long-term architecture can look like this:

Official institutions publish information.

XRPL anchors the proof.

Banks and regulators verify it.

AI consumes it.

Tokenized instruments use it.

Stablecoins and tokenized deposits provide cash.

Institutional markets execute trades.

XRP supplies native network resources and can supply cross-asset liquidity where the route makes sense.

That is not simply a faster payment network.

That starts looking like part of a digital financial operating system.

And then remember where this conversation is happening.

Inside the research world of the institution that measures:

$9.6 trillion of FX turnover every day

plus

$7.9 trillion of interest-rate derivatives turnover every day.

A combined:

$17.5 TRILLION DAILY.

No, that is not XRPL volume.

No, BIS does not process those trades.

The significance is that BIS researchers just tested XRP Ledger while working inside the institutional world surrounding markets of that size.

That is the fact.

And now I’m asking the question that matters to me as an ripple:native holder:

What happens if XRPL earns even a small role inside the tokenized version of that financial system?

Because 0.1% of a trillion-dollar market is not small.

And this market is not one trillion.

It is trillions every single day.

That is why Working Paper 1374 changed the scale of the conversation for me.

For years, people asked whether XRP could become part of the future financial system.

Now researchers inside the BIS have taken XRP Ledger, built institutional infrastructure on it, and explicitly discussed a future combining trusted information with digital money and programmable financial assets.

We are still at the prototype stage.

But for me, the direction is the real story.

The next financial system will need trusted data, tokenized assets, automated execution and deep liquidity.

XRPL is now showing up in all four conversations.

And XRP sits natively underneath the network where those pieces can eventually meet.

$17.5T a day. Now look at your ripple:native bag again. 

Enough?

When the price of a token falls, people do not pocket the savings and use the same amount of intelligence. They spend the surplus on more steps, longer context, extra retries, and jobs that were not worth running at the old price. That is why a collapse in cost per token does not shrink compute demand(like many AI Bears claimed). It multiplies it. A cheap token makes it rational to let an agent reread the repo, call tools, criticize its own draft, and try again, which is the same request a person used to make in one shot, only stretched across ten to fifty model turns. Each of those turns still needs accelerators spinning, memory bandwidth, and power, so the bill per useful outcome can drop while the machines required to deliver it rise. Jevons shows up here in the simplest form: inference got hundreds of times cheaper over a few years, token volume filled the gap, and agents turned that volume into a loop instead of a chat. The 10–50× demand for CPU is not a claim that chips got worse. It is the workload getting thicker because the unit of thought got cheap enough to waste on purpose.

Global Token consumption did not “jump overnight” in February 2026, but that month is the clearest inflection in who is burning the tokens: agents overtook humans on the best public telemetry, and global throughput kept compounding from an already-high base. 

That is +57% in the six months after mid January, or roughly +35% in the first quarter after the Feb inflection, then slower. On the chart, the solid floor is still only ~40–50 T through most of 2025, then steps up hard in late 2025 (China national series entering the ledger: 100 T by Dec 2025, 140 T by Mar 2026) and climbs from ~170 T around Feb ’26 toward ~300 T by June. 

Where Agentic AI actually shows up:

The sharpest agent specific series is OpenRouter (developer/API router, open-weight and tool heavy, not the whole market). Multiple write ups of OpenRouter / a16z data converge on the same story:
~Around 1–6 February 2026, agentic traffic crossed human traffic on the platform.
~Agentic tokens then went from ~0.51 T to ~7.3 T (14×) by mid-August.
~Human tokens grew only ~2.8× over the same window (to ~1.4–1.5 T).
~Agents therefore sit at ~5× human volume on that slice.

That is the operational meaning of “took the main stage.” Humans still ask questions, agents loop: plan → retrieve → tool call → critic → retry, often for hours. OpenRouter also reports tool call rates on some traffic rising from <5% to >25% over ~12 months, and 50%+ of output tokens as internal reasoning in places. Chinese coding/agent models (MiniMax, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek) took a large share of that February surge.

Agents inflate token counts so violently because they do not use a model the way a person does. A human asks a question, gets an answer, and stops. An agent treats that same model as a worker that has to keep going: break the job into steps, pull files or search results, call tools, check whether the result is any good, and try again if it is not. Each of those loops sends the model more text than the last one. The system prompt, the repo, the ticket, the docs, and the running scratchpad all come back again. That is why a task that looks like “fix this bug” can burn hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens while a normal chat uses a few thousand.

The expensive part is usually the input, not the clever paragraph at the end. The model has to reread a large context on every turn even when most of that context has not changed. Caching takes some of the sting out of the bill on instrumented traffic something like seventy to eighty-five percent of agent tokens are repeated prompts billed at a discount but the raw meter still spins. Research on agentic coding makes the gap concrete: those workloads can consume on the order of a thousand times more tokens than ordinary chat and several thousand times more than a single shot reasoning question. Two runs of the same ticket can also differ by an order of magnitude, because the agent wanders, retries, or over explains. Goldman’s shorthand is the same idea in plainer clothes, an agent is a chatbot request blown up ten to fifty times.

That is the February 2026 story underneath the global chart. The planet’s estimated throughput did not suddenly multiply by fourteen. It climbed from roughly two hundred thirty trillion tokens a day in mid January to about three hundred sixty by mid July. What changed composition was who was doing the consuming. On OpenRouter, the slice of the market where developers actually wire models to tools, agents crossed humans around the first week of February and then ran away with the graph: about fourteen times more agent tokens by August, against less than three times growth for people. Agents there now use several times as many tokens as humans. That platform is not the whole world Google’s product surfaces and China’s national totals still dominate the big index but it is the cleanest public picture of the new customer. The customer is no longer only a person typing. It is software that keeps the model on the clock.

China went from almost nothing in early 2024 to an official floor around one hundred forty trillion a day by spring 2026, with other Chinese reports implying the true number may already be higher. Google disclosed on the order of one hundred five trillion a day across first party and partner surfaces. OpenAI and Anthropic have to be inferred from APIs, revenue, and cost, so they sit in wider bands of tens of trillions each. Fireworks and similar hosts add another large pile of open-model serving. 

Costs per token have collapsed for years, and usage has filled every gap that created. Agents are simply the next intensity step: more tokens per useful outcome, not just more people chatting. If the longer forecasts that pin a twenty four times jump by 2030 on agentic demand are even roughly right, the chart you are looking at is the start of that shift, not the peak of it.

The driver is Agentic AI, and AMD already has the densest shipping product for the jobs those agents actually do.

The industry spent the first wave of generative AI treating the CPU as furniture. Training and token generation live on GPUs. Then models started acting: spawning sub agents, calling APIs, writing files, installing packages, compiling code, checking policy, and stuffing tool results back into a context that can run to hundreds of thousands or even a million tokens. That loop is not matrix math. Intel’s Souvik Kundu has said many stages of an agentic task are inherently CPU jobs: parse the output, pick a tool, make the call or run the code, collect the result, feed it back. AMD’s Madhu Rangarajan has gone further in public comments around the same research wave, arguing that in realistic pipelines most stages run entirely on the CPU. The GPU still does inference. Everything around it, the harness, the sandbox, the tokenizer, the guardrails, the enterprise services the agent is allowed to touch, is general purpose compute. That is why hyperscalers and AI Labs are scaling toward 1-2 CPU : 1 GPU.

You can see the strain in the cloud before you see it in a slide deck. AWS told internal engineers to stop wasting CPU cycles after wait times for CPU capacity stretched from hours to days. That is the world’s largest cloud operator treating spare EPYC and Graviton inventory like a scarce resource, not leftover capacity. Distributors report Intel fulfilling only about 40 percent of yearly server CPU backlog in places, with lead times measured in months. Some server CPU prices have jumped more than 40 percent in under a year. Intel has redirected older node wafer starts toward servers and industrial parts, which is another way of saying the money moved. Lip-Bu Tan has described CEOs calling him for more CPUs. When both the volume leader and the share gainer are sold out, the bottleneck is real.

The technical bottleneck is more specific than “agents use computers.” Tokenization is a good example. Converting text into token IDs is branchy, data dependent string work. On a short chat prompt it is cheap. On an agent that keeps appending tool results and then re-tokenizes a 100,000 token running sequence, it is not. Georgia Tech work associated with Euijun Chung found that too few CPU cores leave GPUs idle waiting for the next dispatch, and that adding cores can cut time to first token by roughly 1.5x to 7x on long sequences. Kundu’s group, also tied to Georgia Tech and Intel, showed that GPUs and CPUs take turns sitting idle in agentic pipelines and that better scheduling can cut end to end latency by up to about 1.8x under load. Safety checks often stay on the CPU too, because they are small, rule heavy, and latency sensitive. None of that is a GPU’s favorite job. All of it scales with the number of agents, and agents scale with each other.

This is where AMD’s product shape matches the workload. Fifth generation EPYC Turin already goes to 192 cores. Sixth generation Venice, ramping on TSMC 2 nm, is aimed at 256 cores and 512 threads, with AMD talking about much higher memory bandwidth per socket and a portfolio split on purpose: dense parts for agent sandboxes, high frequency parts to keep GPUs fed as host nodes, and general purpose SKUs for the databases and services agents call. AMD’s own rack modeling current Turin configuration can put more than 27,000 cores in a liquid-cooled rack class and that Venice stretches that toward 36,000-81,000, with modeled 100 kW rack throughput well ahead of Intel’s Granite Rapids and Nvidia’s 88 core Vera baseline. Agentic fleets care about agents per watt, per dollar, and per rack, plus the boring fact that most enterprise tools still speak x86. AMD has been selling that combination into cloud instances that grew about 50 percent to more than 1,600 publicly listed EPYC shapes. Venice demand, Su has said, is stronger than for any prior generation.

$NVDA  Jensen Huang’s line is that agents will be the largest users of computing. If Vera stays tied to Rubin racks and a few hyperscalers, it is a specialist. If it leaks into general CPU servers, AMD’s density argument has to keep winning on software compatibility and cores per rack, not just slides. Arm designs from AWS Graviton5, Qualcomm, and others are also being pitched as orchestration silicon. The field is getting crowded because the money moved.

The uncomfortable part is that a CPU crunch does not stay in the data center. When wafer starts, substrates, and packaging follow server ASPs, client CPUs get rationed, prices rise, and PC makers feel it. Analysts already talk about the shortage trickling into consumer channels the way GPU and HBM shortages did. AMD is following the money too; that is what a winner does. The risk for buyers is simple. Agentic systems multiply work at machine speed. Every extra tool call is more tokenization, more Python, more syscalls, more policy checks. Software can hide some of that with smarter scheduling and incremental tokenizers. It cannot repeal the need for cores, memory bandwidth, and I/O sitting next to the GPU.

Dr. Lisa Su’s EPYC bet only looks obvious now. For years it meant shipping more cores, more memory bandwidth, and a cleaner chiplet design while the industry stared at GPUs. The real wager was simpler than a forecast about agents: the data center would still need a fast, dense, x86 processor to run other people’s software. That is the work agents do once they leave the GPU and start calling tools, compiling code, hitting databases, re-tokenizing long context, and enforcing policy. Turin at 192 cores and Venice aimed at 256 were not built for a keynote slogan. They were built for messy concurrent jobs, and that is suddenly the scarce layer in AI infrastructure.

The market is paying her back in the dull numbers. AMD now takes close to half of x86 server processor revenue while still shipping fewer units than Intel, cloud catalogs keep adding EPYC instances, and Dr. Su can guide server CPU growth above 80 percent in the second half of 2026 because customers raised their own CPU plans first. EPYC is already the high volume way to run the non-GPU half of an agent fleet without a software rewrite. She did not need to predict agentic AI in 2017. She needed to keep the unglamorous compute layer excellent until the next wave of software ran into it. It did.

Editorial: “Unkind cuts” — ECI’s voter deletions

Core Idea

Editorial questions the large-scale deletion of voters during the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka.

1. Scale of deletions

Around 22% voters in Telangana and 19.5% in Karnataka were reportedly deleted.

Bengaluru saw some constituencies losing more than half their electors.

Hyderabad had several constituencies with over 40% deletions.

Such massive deletions cannot simply be dismissed as routine cleaning of electoral rolls.

2. Why is it problematic?

If voters have merely migrated within the same State, their names should be shifted rather than deleted.

The editorial argues that available survey and population data do not sufficiently justify such large reductions.

Therefore, transparency + verification become essential.

3. Democratic concern

The right to vote is central to universal adult franchise.
Wrongful deletion can lead to disenfranchisement—a citizen being effectively excluded from democratic participation.

4. Institutional accountability

ECI has reportedly not provided adequate elector-to-population ratios and detailed deletion data.

Karnataka’s deletion lists lacked easily verifiable details such as old booth numbers, making verification difficult.

Political parties and citizens also need to actively file objections.

5. Larger lesson

Electoral-roll revision is necessary to remove dead, duplicate or shifted voters, but the process must never sacrifice legitimate voters.

Way Forward:
Transparency → searchable deletion lists → door-to-door verification → easy claims & objections → independent audit → timely restoration of wrongly deleted names.
